lesson.title: The Insulator That Makes Capacitors Better: Dielectrics
lesson.summary: The insulating material between a capacitor's plates, the dielectric, boosts how much charge it stores and sets the voltage it can safely survive.
lesson.body:
The gap between a capacitor's two plates is never actually empty in a practical component. It is filled with an insulating material called a dielectric, and the choice of that material has an enormous effect on how much charge the capacitor can store. A dielectric does not conduct electricity, so it still blocks charge from crossing directly between the plates, but its molecules respond to the electric field sitting across the gap. Many dielectric molecules are polar, meaning they have a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, and the applied field twists them into partial alignment, a process called polarization. That alignment creates a small opposing field inside the material, which partially cancels the field from the plates' own charge. The result is that, for the same charge on the plates, the voltage across the capacitor ends up lower than with a vacuum gap, and since capacitance is charge divided by voltage, a lower voltage for the same charge means a higher capacitance.

This boosting effect is captured by the relative permittivity, often called the dielectric constant and written epsilon-r, which you met in the capacitance formula as the multiplier on epsilon-zero. Vacuum defines the baseline at exactly 1, and air is close enough to treat as 1 for most purposes. Paper sits around 2 to 4 depending on how it is processed, mica runs roughly 5 to 7, and the oxide layers used inside electrolytic capacitors run higher still, often in the range of 7 to 10. Ceramic dielectrics span the widest range of all, from around 10 up into the thousands for specially formulated high-permittivity ceramics, which is exactly why small ceramic capacitors can pack surprisingly large capacitance values into tiny packages.

Return to the parallel plate capacitor from the capacitance chapter: 100 square centimeters of plate area, a 1 millimeter gap, which gave 88.54 picofarads with air filling the gap. Now replace that air with a mica sheet, epsilon-r around 5, keeping the geometry identical. The new capacitance is simply the old value multiplied by epsilon-r, so 88.54 picofarads times 5 equals 442.7 picofarads, roughly five times more storage from the same physical size, purely from swapping the insulating material.

A dielectric does more than raise capacitance, though. It also physically separates the plates so they cannot touch and short together, and it must survive the electric field pressing across it without breaking down. Every dielectric has a dielectric strength, a maximum field, in volts per meter, it can withstand before it fails, arcs through, and permanently damages the capacitor. This is why every real capacitor carries a voltage rating: exceed that rating and the field across the thin dielectric can exceed its breakdown strength, punching a conductive channel through the material and destroying the part, sometimes violently in electrolytic types.

Manufacturers choose dielectrics to hit different tradeoffs among capacitance, size, voltage rating, and stability. Ceramic capacitors use compressed ceramic powders and dominate small, low-value, high-frequency applications. Film capacitors use thin plastic sheets like polyester or polypropylene, favored where stability and low loss matter more than sheer size. Electrolytic and tantalum capacitors grow an extremely thin oxide layer electrochemically on a metal foil or pellet, and because that layer stays thin without breaking down, these capacitors pack the largest capacitance values, often thousands of microfarads, into a small can, at the cost of requiring correct polarity.
